title: Race conditions and thread safety
description: Identify race conditions, understand memory ordering, and apply thread-safe patterns in C#.

data.text: When multiple threads access shared data without coordination, the result depends on the exact timing of each thread. This is a *race condition* — and it is one of the most common sources of elusive production bugs.
What a race condition looks like

Imagine two threads incrementing the same counter. The increment operation is not atomic: it reads the value, adds one, and writes back. If both threads read the same value before either writes back, one increment is silently lost.

data.title: Race condition on a shared counter

data.text: Modern CPUs and compilers reorder instructions for performance. Without synchronization, one thread may not see changes made by another thread in time. The `volatile` keyword and `Thread.MemoryBarrier()` provide limited ordering guarantees, but they do not make compound operations atomic.

data.text: `volatile` prevents certain compiler and CPU reordering, but it does not make `counter++` safe. For compound operations like read-modify-write, use `lock` or `Interlocked`.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Race conditions happen when unsynchronized threads share mutable state.
`Interlocked` makes simple operations atomic without a lock.
`volatile` controls visibility but does not make operations atomic.
Use `lock` when multiple operations must happen together as a unit.
